transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-19
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Li (Redwood SE), Ellen Kim (Redwood Partner Ops); Daniel Ortiz (VelaScale Head of Partnerships), Priya Menon (Infra Lead), Jasper Ng (BizDev), Lena Rossi (Security)

Summary (auto): Quick partner intro between Redwood and VelaScale to explore reseller/managed infra partnership. Discussed common customer profiles, GPU roadmap, workload characteristics, security/compliance constraints, and next steps for tech deep dive and joint benchmarks.

Topics: introductions, partnership models (resell vs co-sell), hardware roadmap (A100->H100 equivalence), private deployment options (VPC/on-prem), SOC2 & KMS, benchmarking plan, commercial handshake

Action items (captured): see metadata above

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Sofia from Redwood, AE on the partnerships team. Marcus, do you want to quickly introduce?
[00:10] Marcus Li: Yep, Marcus Li, solutions engineer. I work on runtime perf and private deployments. Hi all.
[00:15] Daniel Ortiz: Daniel here, head of partnerships at VelaScale. Thanks for the invite. We're excited to learn more.
[00:20] Priya Menon: Priya, infra lead. We manage their ML infra and procurement for customers who need managed GPU clusters.
[00:25] Jasper Ng: Jasper, bizdev, looking for go-to-market motions and revenue splits.
[00:30] Lena Rossi: Lena, security. I'll be scanning for compliance fit and data flow.
[00:35] Sofia Park: Great, thanks. Quick agenda — intros, what each company is looking for in a partner, technical fit, then next steps. Does that work?
[00:45] Daniel Ortiz: Sounds good. Quick context from VelaScale: we provide managed GPU infra and want to integrate a turnkey inference runtime and marketplace for customers who need low-latency LLM serving. We're exploring two paths: a tight reseller integration where we offer Redwood-backed inference as an add-on, or deeper technical OEM where we run Redwood Private on our clusters.
[01:05] Marcus Li: Perfect. From Redwood's perspective, we do hosted API, dedicated reserved capacity, and private deployments. For partners like you we typically do either a co-sell + reseller package or a private deployment where you run our control plane or local runtime with your infra.
[01:18] Priya Menon: On the infra side, our customers run varied workloads — some chatbots at high QPS with p50 seq lengths ~64 tokens; others are embedding pipelines with long contexts, up to 4k tokens p95. We care about deterministic latency at p95 and cost predictability.
[01:36] Marcus Li: Okay that's helpful. Do you have typical batch sizes and concurrency? That impacts kernel selection and batching strategy.
[01:44] Priya Menon: For high QPS chat it's small batches, often batch size 1-4. For embedding pipelines we can batch up to 32 but latency SLOs are looser.
[01:54] Jasper Ng: From a commercial lens, we want to understand margins if we resell Redwood — and whether there's white-labeling or API keys per customer.
[02:05] Ellen Kim: We can discuss partner pricing and reseller margins. There's a partner ops playbook we can share. White-labeling is limited from a security/branding perspective but we often support co-branded portals.
[02:16] Daniel Ortiz: Good. One of our customers insisted on SSO, SAML, and detailed audit logs. How does Redwood handle SSO in private deployments?
[02:25] Marcus Li: For private we've integrated with customer SAML/Okta flows and can federate identities. Audit logs and KMS integrations are supported; for on-prem we can point to local HSM/KMS with envelope encryption.
[02:37] Lena Rossi: Do you have SOC 2 or ISO certs for the hosted product? If we're reselling hosted to enterprise customers, they'd ask.
[02:44] Sofia Park: Yes, hosted Redwood is SOC 2 Type II. We also have SOC/ISO artifacts for enterprise and can arrange redacted reports under NDA.
[02:52] Priya Menon: Reservation capacity — if we run Redwood on our clusters, do you support autoscaling and burst to cloud? Some customers want hybrid bursts.
[03:02] Marcus Li: We support autoscaling policies and can configure burst to compatible cloud regions. Hybrid bursting requires routing rules and network peering; it's doable but needs a networking design session.
[03:12] Daniel Ortiz: Let's talk hardware. We mostly use a mix of A100 80GB and H100 nodal offerings. Do you have perf profiles per model/quantization for H100?
[03:23] Marcus Li: We maintain a model catalog with verified performance profiles; for H100 we generally see a 1.3-1.6x improvement for transformer decoder workloads vs A100 depending on sequence length and kernel path. Quantization to 4-bit or 8-bit gives big throughput gains but depends on model fidelity requirements.
[03:38] Priya Menon: Any known issues with KV cache persistence across private deployments? Some of our customers need session continuity across nodes.
[03:48] Marcus Li: We have KV cache sharding approaches and sticky routing for long-context sessions. If redundancy is required we can persist to a fast shared store but that impacts latency. Tradeoff conversation.
[04:00] Jasper Ng: From a time-to-market perspective, how long does a private deployment take? Weeks? Months?
[04:07] Sofia Park: For a basic private deployment with a small cluster and our control plane, typical timeline is 4-6 weeks including security reviews and networking. A deeper OEM integration may be 2-3 months.
[04:18] Daniel Ortiz: On pricing, are there committed reserved capacity models? We want to offer predictable pricing to our customers.
[04:25] Sofia Park: Yes, Redwood Dedicated supports monthly/annual commits and reserved GPU pools for guaranteed throughput. We can map dispatch to your pricing model.
[04:33] Priya Menon: How do you measure cost per token/embedding when mixed workloads run on same cluster?
[04:39] Marcus Li: We provide token-level cost and latency breakdowns in the console and per-route dashboards. For partner deployments we'd expose usage metrics so you can bill customers by route or model.
[04:50] Lena Rossi: Security question: if we run Redwood Private, where are customer logs stored and who has access? For compliance we need separation of duties.
[04:58] Marcus Li: Logs can be forwarded to your central logging with RBAC controls; access is managed by your identity provider. We can set role-scoped permissions and audit trails.
[05:08] Daniel Ortiz: Have you done partner benchmarks before? We're particularly interested in cold-starts and tail latency.
[05:15] Marcus Li: Yes, we can run controlled benchmarks. Typical deliverables: p50/p95/p99 latencies for representative prompts, throughput curves, and token cost estimates. We'll need a sample workload and access to a test cluster.
[05:27] Priya Menon: Ok, if we do a technical deep dive, we want to include our network team because of firewall/NAT concerns.
[05:34] Sofia Park: Makes sense — we'll include networking in the deep dive invitation.
[05:38] Daniel Ortiz: On GTM, we want clarity on lead ownership and SLAs. If we resell, who owns support tickets?
[05:46] Ellen Kim: We typically do co-managed support for reseller partners, with incident routing rules. Level 1 triage can be done by VelaScale, and Redwood handles platform-level escalations. We can define SLAs in the partner MSA.
[05:58] Jasper Ng: Any notable integrations for billing and metering we should know — like chargeback APIs?
[06:05] Marcus Li: We expose usage APIs with token-level detail; partners can pull per-customer usage for billing.
[06:10] Daniel Ortiz: Cool. Sounds promising. Quick product note: we have a few customers testing LLMs on quantized weights and some strict latency SLOs — is Redwood's runtime friendly to INT4/INT8 kernels?
[06:20] Marcus Li: Yes, runtime supports quantization-friendly execution paths, and we have recommendations per workload. But INT4/8 tradeoffs need evals — we often suggest A/B quality checks against unquantized baselines.
[06:33] Priya Menon: If customers require data residency in EU, is private the only option?
[06:38] Sofia Park: Hosted can be regionally isolated in EU regions with data residency controls, but for strict legal requirements private/on-prem is recommended.
[06:46] Lena Rossi: We'll likely need a redacted SOC2 and some architecture diagrams.
[06:50] Sofia Park: We'll send those under NDA.
[06:53] Daniel Ortiz: Great. Let's talk timing: we'd like a benchmark and tech deep dive next week if possible.
[06:59] Marcus Li: I can do a technical deep dive week of 7/26 — available Wed/Thu. We can reserve benchmark windows after we get the workload profile.
[07:08] Priya Menon: Wed 7/28 afternoon works on our side.
[07:12] Sofia Park: I'll follow up with calendar invites and include the networking and security folks.
[07:16] Jasper Ng: For commercial chemistry, we want partner margins and an MSA — what's the next step?
[07:22] Ellen Kim: We'll send a partner one-pager with pricing anchors and an outline of the reseller/partner MSA. Legal intro will follow.
[07:29] Daniel Ortiz: One more technical point — we sometimes need model pinning with rollbacks in case of regressions. Does Redwood support rollout/rollback policies?
[07:37] Marcus Li: Yes, rollouts, canary deploys, A/B tests, and automatic fallback policies are supported in the platform. We also tie evals to prompt sets for regression alerts.
[07:48] Priya Menon: That's a big plus.
[07:51] Sofia Park: Ok to recap and assign next steps?
[07:55] Daniel Ortiz: Go ahead.
[07:57] Sofia Park: Recap — Redwood to send partner deck, pricing anchors, SOC2/arch docs under NDA; Marcus to schedule tech deep dive week of 7/26 (target Wed 7/28); VelaScale to share workload profile; run benchmark windows after profile arrives; set up legal intro for partner MSA.
[08:18] Daniel Ortiz: That matches our expectations. Thanks everyone.
[08:22] Sofia Park: Thanks all. We'll follow up via email and include the action items.
[08:26] Meeting end.

Notes on transcription: some names may be transcribed imperfectly; timestamps approximate. The call included short cross-talk and quick clarifications.
